summary: The loop can now drive the real editor from a JSON script: open a capture, press keys, click and drag, render the window offscreen, and read back what the editor did. The next audit edits a script instead of rebuilding a throwaway harness, and the walk it produces is repeatable.
setup: Nothing to install. From the repo: Scripts/playtest.sh Scripts/playtest/redline-walk.json. It builds and launches the probe app (not your dev app), runs the walk invisibly, prints done.json, and quits the probe. Output lands in /tmp/photonz-playtest/redline-walk.

try.do: Run Scripts/playtest.sh Scripts/playtest/redline-walk.json and watch it finish in about 15 seconds with status ok and 69 steps.
Open /tmp/photonz-playtest/redline-walk/3-distance-placed.png. This is the editor after two clicks and a third to place the number.
Open 4-size-landed.png, then 5-gap-landed.png and 6-align-landed.png: one Size click, one Gap click, one Alignment drag.
Open 7-arrow-captioned.png: an arrow drawn with A, captioned by typing and Return.
Open log.json and find the 8-spec entry: the spec list the walk copied, with every measurement named and valued.
Change one point in Scripts/playtest/redline-walk.json (for example the Size click to the Reset button at [136, 786]) and run it again with --no-build.
Read docs/design/playtest-harness.md for the full step list.

evaluate: Is a JSON script the right level for the next audit to work at, or would you rather the loop wrote Swift again?
Do the offscreen renders show enough of the window to judge a feature by, given glass and vibrancy do not render?
Is the per-step editor state in log.json (tool, mode, hint, measurements, clipboard) the state you would want to read when a walk goes wrong?
Should the harness also drive the capture overlay and the toast, or is the editor enough for now?
rough: Menu shortcuts that act on the focused editor (Copy as Spec List, Copy Image) do nothing in a scripted run, because the probe is never the active app and its focused editor is nil. The log says so; the walk uses direct actions for the outcome.
The probe remembers its last Measure mode between runs, so a walk has to say which mode it wants. The example does; a script that assumes a fresh state will drift.
The capture overlay and the post-capture toast are not scriptable yet. The walk starts at the editor.

The walk exposed two product findings, now queued: Size mode names its calipers Gap when the style role was spacing, and the selected caliper's midpoint handle sits on top of its number right after placement.
